component.name: Time Warp Studio
component.summary: An old-school programming environment with ten languages

description.p: Time Warp Studio is a workbench for old-school programming: BASIC, APL, Logo, PILOT, FOCAL, Scheme, COMAL, REXX, Smalltalk and Forth in one window, each with an editor, a debugger and turtle graphics. Every language runs natively inside the application.
A checked curriculum of 20 lessons and 60 checkpoints ships with it for teaching, and the whole application is offline: it makes no network call of its own unless you configure the assistant.

The IDE and the languages, and nothing else. The three emulated machines are removed — the HB-1 home computer, the HB-2 of 1992 and the CHIP-8 virtual machine, with the language that ran on it — along with their windows, their manuals, their examples, their test suites and their gates. The ten languages, the editor, the turtle canvas, the debugger, the lessons, the assistant and the automation surface are unchanged.

The HB-2's last three gaps close. Nine of the Studio's languages run on the machine's own bus through a ROM socket, so a BASIC POKE writes video memory and SYS calls its processor; a cassette sits beside the disk, with a tape head that only goes forward; and the joystick registers answer STICK and STRIG from a real gamepad. An assembler defect that a two-ORG listing could turn into a four-gigabyte allocation is fixed with them.

The HB-2 becomes a machine you can use: a window with the machine's screen and keyboard, HB DOS 2.0 with directories and sector accounting, eight processes on a desktop, a monitor, a module bay and a prompt. And the Studio is Linux only, with no build or installer for any other system.

The HB-2: the HB-1's 1992 successor, with a bus that keeps the 1982 map as MODE 0, a 640 x 480 framebuffer with a blitter and sprites, four channels of sampled audio, and HB-16 -- its own processor, with an assembler, a disassembler and sixteen operating-system services. Headless, with a harness and six demonstration programs.

Closing the window asks about the split's documents too, a file open on the right is raised rather than opened twice, autosave and the unsaved marker cover both panes, and the tab menu's Duplicate, Copy File Path and Open Containing Folder entries do something.
Close Other Tabs and Close All Tabs work, a document on the split's right-hand side is saved before it closes, and the guides state the number of programs and suites the tree actually has.
The terminal cannot stall the window, has Interrupt and Restart, names input it could not deliver, and a background run replaces its own notification instead of stacking a second one.

A real pseudo-terminal in the Terminal tab, three historical voices for the assistant, a desktop notification when a run finishes behind you, an original five-page tour the CHIP-8 boots into, a curated CC0 homebrew archive behind one button, and this Flatpak.
CHIP-8 runs can be walked back. This is the last release built for Windows and macOS, and it is archived.
